summary:
LUNOVA is an interactive lunar mission trainer that turns space science into a hands-on experience for young explorers. Players manage a small Moon base and protect four astronauts by balancing energy, water, oxygen, food production, and shelter during a solar event.

Developed as a browser-based 3D simulation, LUNOVA addresses the challenge by making life-support systems interdependent: every decision has costs, constraints, and visible consequences. Players can review resource graphs, understand their mission’s outcome, and test alternative decision paths. A science journal connects the experience to NASA sources, including a historical solar event from DONKI, while clearly distinguishing real observations from simulation assumptions.

LUNOVA brings complex systems to life through exploration and experimentation. Multilingual content, guided tutorials, accessibility options, and mobile support help more learners participate. Educator tools support classroom and exhibition use without requiring player accounts. By encouraging curiosity, evidence-based reasoning, and reflection, LUNOVA is designed to help learners understand why sustaining life beyond Earth requires cooperation and careful resource management.
details:
LUNOVA — Your choices keep the mission alive

LUNOVA is an interactive lunar outpost simulation developed for the Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. Players take responsibility for four astronauts and discover how energy, water, oxygen, food production, and protection depend on one another.

The experience combines a navigable 3D environment, consequential decisions, scientific references, and opportunities to revisit choices. Its central question is simple: how do you keep a mission alive when every system depends on limited resources?

Project objectives

LUNOVA aims to:

  • Make the challenges of sustaining life beyond Earth understandable through play.
  • Help learners recognize connections between life-support systems.
  • Encourage decisions based on resource availability and observable consequences.
  • Connect space exploration to authentic NASA observations and research.
  • Support experimentation by allowing players to compare alternative decisions.
  • Give educators and institutions a configurable activity for different learning environments.

How the experience works

Players explore a small lunar base inhabited by Alex, Maya, Rio, and Sam. They allocate electricity, choose an infrastructure improvement, manage operations, respond to a solar event, and plan recovery.

Selecting an option highlights the relevant module, connecting the decision to the physical layout of the base. A persistent dashboard displays resource reserves throughout the mission.

The simulation makes dependencies visible:

  • Cultivation requires electricity and water.
  • Water recycling depends on available power.
  • Expanding a battery increases its capacity without immediately filling it.
  • Actions with unaffordable upfront costs become unavailable.
  • Warnings explain potential shortages and their consequences.

Simulated time advances when decisions are confirmed. Players can read, discuss, and explore without a countdown.

At the end, a contextual conclusion explains the outcome. Resource graphs and a decision history help players understand what changed. They can then modify one or more choices and compare an alternative path under the same initial conditions and external events, while preserving their original trajectory.

Scientific foundations

LUNOVA connects gameplay to documented sources while distinguishing observations from simulation assumptions.

  • NASA DONKI: a verified historical solar energetic particle event provides context for the mission’s alert.
  • OSDR RadLab: radiation observations support an interactive data-exploration activity.
  • NASA Open Science Data Repository: selected plant studies introduce research on cultivation conditions and biological responses.
  • NASA Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document: specific reference values inform oxygen consumption and drinking-water requirements.

    The Science journal explains these connections and links to the original sources. Historical observations are preserved with provenance information. Gameplay parameters, such as equipment capacities, preparation intervals, and the shelter-protection indicator, are identified as educational assumptions.

The application does not present its simplified model as an operational mission-planning tool or a prediction of lunar radiation exposure.

Designed for schools, museums, and learning spaces

LUNOVA is designed for use by:

  • Schools and educators.
  • Museums and science centers.
  • Planetariums and public exhibitions.
  • Science outreach programs and facilitated workshops.
  • Families and independent learners.

Participants can play without creating an account. Guided, express, and self-paced modes support different levels of mediation and available time.

A separate, authenticated administrative area enables institutions to personalize the activity. Authorized staff can:

  • Create and manage experiences.
  • Configure mission mode, language, and accessibility preferences.
  • Organize stations for tablets, computers, and shared kiosks.
  • Share activities through public links and QR codes.
  • Review aggregated participation, decisions, and reflection responses.
  • Manage institutional and staff access according to their permissions.

This administrative area is implemented and functional, but access is not currently available through the public demonstration.

Accessibility and practical use

The design considers different devices, reading preferences, and interaction needs:

  • English, Portuguese, and Spanish.
  • Contextual tutorials that can be reopened at any time.
  • Keyboard navigation.
  • Adjustable text, high contrast, and reduced motion.
  • A playable textual alternative to the 3D environment.
  • Responsive layouts for computers, tablets, and phones.
  • Prepared offline access to public content, with queued decisions synchronized after reconnection.

These features are intended to reduce barriers to participation. Further evaluation with learners, educators, and assistive-technology users remains part of the project’s development.


Technologies and development tools

  • TypeScript and JavaScript: application logic and simulation rules.
  • React and Next.js: interface and application architecture.
  • Three.js and React Three Fiber: interactive 3D rendering and procedural lunar models.
  • HTML and CSS: responsive layouts, interface styling, and animations.
  • PostgreSQL and Prisma: persistent records and database access.
  • Better Auth: authentication for administrative users.
  • Docker Compose: application packaging and deployment.
  • Vitest: automated simulation and application-logic tests.
  • Playwright and axe-core: browser-flow testing and automated accessibility checks.
  • Git and GitHub: version control and repository management.
  • OpenAI Codex: assistance with implementation, debugging, and test development.

The simulation uses explicit, deterministic rules to calculate outcomes. The experience runs in a browser and requires no dedicated headset or specialized controller.

Creativity and intended impact

LUNOVA connects a human story to visible infrastructure and inspectable evidence. Players care for a named crew while discovering how decisions affect the systems that sustain them.

Its alternative-path comparison turns the conclusion into another opportunity for exploration: players can question their first solution, change their approach, and examine the difference.

The intended impact is to encourage curiosity, systems thinking, resource awareness, and evidence-based discussion. Scientific transparency, accessibility, participant privacy, device performance, and institutional flexibility guided the design.

The current prototype provides a working lunar scenario. Learning outcomes and suitability across the challenge’s target ages still require evaluation with children and educators. LUNOVA offers a foundation for that work through a repeatable cycle of exploring, deciding, observing, and trying again.
